title: Review: Carbon cycle and climate change; Conservation and threats to biodiversity; Human impact and sustainability; Classification and phylogeny
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EV08a#t3 term and clue written for the game; EV08b#t1 term and clue written for the game; EV06a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EV06a#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC05c#N.2, EC08#N.23a, EV06a#N.7, EV08b#N.19, EC05c#N.16, EV06a#N.9, EV08b#N.8, EV06a#N.12. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Pollution
items.clue: Threat posed by pesticides and plastics

items.label: Keystone species
items.clue: An organism whose loss changes the whole community

items.label: Taxon
items.clue: Any one group in the hierarchy, such as a family or an order

items.label: Genus
items.clue: First word of a scientific name, written with a capital letter

questions.stem: The bird species of a mountain in New Guinea were surveyed in 1965 and again in 2012. For most species both the upper and the lower limits of the altitudinal range had moved upslope, by about 100 m on average, over a period in which the region warmed. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The species have expanded their ranges, since they now occupy about 100 m more of the mountain.
Because both limits moved equally, the species have lost none of their habitat area.
The correlation between warming and the shift proves that no other factor was involved.
The ranges of the species shifted upslope, tracking the rise in temperature.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. A seaweed bed with a biomass of 5000 tonnes is harvested for food. Each year, growth adds 30% to the biomass and natural losses remove 10%. The current harvest is 1400 tonnes per year. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Sustainable: the harvest of 1400 tonnes is below the 1500 tonnes added each year by growth.
Unsustainable: it exceeds the net replacement of 1000 tonnes a year, so the bed will shrink.
Sustainable: seaweed is a renewable resource that regrows every year, so the bed cannot be used up.
Unsustainable only above 2000 tonnes a year, the total of growth plus natural losses.

questions.stem: Which statement about the scientific name of the tiger, Panthera tigris, is correct?

options.text: The second word, tigris, is on its own enough to identify the species of tiger.
It should be written Panthera Tigris, because both of its words are proper nouns.
Panthera names the genus and tigris distinguishes the species within it.
Panthera tigris and Panthera leo are varieties of one species and interbreed freely.

questions.explanation: First word, genus; second word, the species within that genus. Panthera leo, the lion, shares the genus and has similar traits.

questions.stem: A rare orchid survives in one wild meadow. Its seeds are now stored in a seed bank, and plants grow in a botanic garden. The meadow is due to be ploughed. Orchid seeds need a particular soil fungus to germinate. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The orchid is now secure, because its seeds and living plants are held safely ex situ.
The meadow should be fenced and left alone, as keeping people out is all that a reserve needs.
The meadow should still be protected and managed, as ex situ stocks cannot replace the habitat or its fungus.
Seed banks can store any plant's seeds for ever, so the orchid can be regrown wherever it is wanted.

questions.stem: A hypothetical small mammal lives only in cool meadows near the top of an isolated mountain. Over 40 years the region warms by 1.5 °C. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Its range expands, because warmer conditions open up more of the mountain to it.
Individuals change their genes to suit the warmer climate, so the species stays where it is.
It loses its lower slopes, and its range shrinks towards the summit.
It moves upslope with no loss, as the same band of temperature is still found higher up.

questions.explanation: The cool band shifts up, but a mountain narrows towards the top, so the area left shrinks. An isolated summit leaves nowhere cooler to go: local extinction is a real risk.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a classification in which every group corresponds to evolutionary relationships?

options.text: The groups show which of the organisms are the most advanced.
Every species is given a unique name made up of two parts.
Organisms that look alike are placed together for identification.
Characteristics of members of a group can be predicted.

questions.explanation: When all members of a group evolved from one common ancestor, they share inherited features, so a member's features can be predicted.

questions.stem: A zoo has bred a rare antelope for 30 years from six founding animals. Which is the strongest scientific concern about releasing their descendants into the wild?

options.text: They are safe in the zoo, so release is not needed to secure the species.
Mutations will have given them alleles for zoo life, which they cannot lose again.
Being so numerous after 30 years, the herd must have regained the genetic diversity it started with.
Six founders carried few alleles, so the herd has little genetic variety to meet disease or change.

questions.explanation: Six founders carry few alleles, and inbreeding adds to the problem. Studbooks slow the loss, but cannot replace missing alleles.

questions.stem: The raven is Corvus corax, the rook is Corvus frugilegus and the magpie is Pica pica. What can be concluded from these names alone?

options.text: Raven and rook are two species of one genus, likely closer to each other than to the magpie.
The raven and the rook are one species, because the first word of their names, Corvus, is the same.
The word corax on its own is enough to name the raven in any country and in any language.
The first words say nothing about how the birds are related, so only the second words are needed.
